utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can somebody remind me where are we? Are you still cross-examining, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, the statement of 1999, you say that when the war broke out in Croatia, at the beginning, propaganda was spread on the radio which fanned the flames. You said that questions were put in radio shows such as, "What do you think about Franjo Tudjman?" And you say the shows were designed to heat up the nationalistic feelings of the Serbs, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, aren't you supposed to be cross-examining on Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but yesterday, with leave of the Chamber, I was given leave to raise issues that were mentioned by the Prosecution but were not in the statement disclosed to the Defence. The entire testimony of the witness yesterday contained facts that are almost absent in the statement, 90 per cent of his testimony referred to new issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question you just put is in the statement. I don't remember it being canvassed yesterday by the Prosecutor but it is in the statement so it couldn't be one of the questions raised by the Prosecutor which are not in the statement. Can we please stay on what we are supposed to do? We have got to finish this case as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, you stated that the chief of the SUP in Bosanski Novi was a Serb whose last name was Umicevic and who was a just man but was later killed by the Serbs. It's all in your statement. On page 5 of your statement, you said that in the spring of 1992, a meeting or a rally -- a meeting was held of the trade union representatives in Sarajevo, that Umicevic was the chief of police, and that he strongly advocated a unified police, and that several days later he was killed in Bosanski Novi. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, when Mr. Krupic is asked whether it is correct from his statement, he needs to have the statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have the statement in front of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To jog your memory, Witness, on page 3 of your statement, dating from 1999, you spoke about Mr. Umicevic, the chief of the SUP, whom you said was a just man, who was later killed by the Serbs, and on page 5 of your statement, you say, "and he was strongly in favour of remaining a unified police force," referring to the meeting in spring of 1992. A few days later he was killed in Bosanski Novi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to clarify this, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I attended the meeting of the republican police union because I was a shop steward from my police station in Bosanski Novi. Before going to this meeting, I was sitting with the late Mr. Umicevic and we were discussing the issues such as the division of the police and that was to be the topic of the meeting in Sarajevo. He firmly adhered to the standpoint that the police should never be divided along ethnic lines. These were the positions I advocated in public at the police union meeting in Sarajevo. All the police stations of the then Bosnia-Herzegovina voted for a unified police force, except for Drvar and Grahovo. These were the only two police stations that expressed a desire to divide the police. Mr. Umicevic was a true democrat. He was not a man who supported ethnic divisions. He was in favour of multi-ethnicity, and the very fact that after his murder, on the day of his funeral, on the left bank of the river Una, one could hear shooting in celebration, in joy, and that in itself shows who it was that killed him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you link the death of Mr. Umicevic to his advocating a unified police force?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Umicevic was in the way of certain lobbies. He was an obstacle to them. His murder, I cannot say whether it was done on purpose or out of negligence, but it is a fact that the man disappeared in the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also said that Mr. Umicevic happened to be in a cafe when there was some kind of fight that broke out, that he came to this cafe and was sitting with the cafe owner. As it was reservists who were fighting among themselves, the military police arrived and a shot -- a stray shot hit him.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Wednesday. I think it was the 8th or the 10th of February 1992. I'm almost sure it was the 8th. He was on his way home from work and, as he lived in the same building where this cafe was, and there had already been fights in that cafe between the cafe owner and the reservists from the SAO Krajina, so he went into the cafe to see what was going on. As he knew the cafe owner, he sat down with him in order to see what was going on and what the conflict was about. In the meantime Nikola Krneta, who had before that engaged in a fight with the cafe owner, went to Matijevici to fetch his machine-gun and returned and fired shots into the cafe from outside and hit Mr. Umicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I really don't want to interfere with your cross-examining but I don't see how these questions relate to the Red Berets, and when these questions are issues that were contained in the witness's statement, a copy of which you were supplied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all the matters that the witness is talking about are things that the Defence wishes to check, in order to see whether the killing of the police chief in Bosanski Novi was linked to some kind of plan to have other forces take power in Bosanski Novi, whether it was the Serb forces, whether it was the SDS, whether even Serbs who opposed this were eliminated. That's what I'm attempting to check. I will -- I will now finish this topic; however, I have no further questions about it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't dispute what you want to check. That is what you may want to check. But the procedure is that when this witness comes as a 92 bis witness, he's going to be cross-examined only on the Red Berets. The only exception was to deal with issues that were raised by the Prosecutor which were not contained in the witness's statement. You are now dealing with issues that are in the witness's statement, which are not related to Red Berets. That's all I'm saying to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please keep relevant before we start having to rule questions out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about how Hrvatska Kostajnica fell into Serb hands when answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor yesterday. You stated that you went to Bosanska Kostajnica where the Croatian members of the Croatian MUP were crossing the bridge and handing over their weapons on the Bosnian side. You said they were putting their weapons on a pile and that local Serb civilians took those weapons in the presence of the army and the police. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that a certain policeman from Knin called Popovic was the man disarming the Croatian policemen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether his last name was Popovic or Ivanovic. I think it was Ivanovic. His first name was Goran. He was searching those men and taking them to a local community centre or cinema or something of that sort and there, they robbed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 6, in paragraph 2, that's the statement from 1999, you say that the SDS openly armed the citizens of Serb ethnicity in Bosanski Novi and that the Territorial Defence of Bosanski Novi had disarmed 380 Croat police. Which of these two statements is correct? First, it was stated that the Serb policemen from Knin disarmed these Croat policemen and here you say it was the Territorial Defence of Bosanski Novi that did that.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify that, Your Honours. As regards the arming of the Serb people, it's an indisputable fact that it was the former JNA who armed the Serb population, both in towns and in villages. I socialised with Serbs. I had more Serb friends than Muslim friends, because I happened to live in such an environment. And my friends told me that weapons had been offered to them and even if they said they didn't want weapons, they were told they would be expelled from Bosanski Novi if they didn't take them. As for the surrender of the policemen in Bosanska Kostajnica, they were crossing the bridge and on the right-hand side of the bridge looking from the direction of Hrvatska Kostajnica, they took off their weapons and threw them on a pile. It was already twilight, dusk. Villagers, local people, approached the pile and took weapons. Martic's police, under the leadership of either Ivanovic or Popovic, whom I knew personally and whom I saw, and I heard from my colleagues that they were practically only observers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to be perfectly clear on what you're talking about, was that the situation when after the fighting in Croatia, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, in Hrvatska Kostajnica, there was a defeat of the Croat forces and then they crossed over to the Bosnian side and surrendered weapons? Is that the event that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking to -- I'm talking about what happened when there was a conflict in SAO Krajina and when the members of the MUP remained under siege in Hrvatska Kostajnica. Since they had no further supplies, no food, nothing, they decided to surrender, and I know that one of their doctors, during of the course of the day crossed over with a white flag and that is when they indeed surrendered after negotiations. They surrendered by the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you speak slowly, please, Mr. Krupic when you testify? I hear the interpreter really rattling very fast trying to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood what you were saying, Mr. Krupic, what is written on page 6 of your statement is not correct, that is that they were disarmed by the Territorial Defence of Bosanski Novi but rather it was done by these people that you're talking about, this Popovic or whatever his last name may be?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO was there. The TO of Bosanski Novi. They were in Bosanska Kostajnica, but I am talking about the search of persons and the seizure of valuables, including jewellery. This was done by the group headed by Ivanovic. I think Ivanovic was the name. Whereas the TO was present and they organised the surrender itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please listen to what I'm asking you, Mr. Krupic. The disarming of the Croatian MUP was carried out by the Territorial Defence of Bosanski Novi. That's what you confirmed just now; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what I should call this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, the Prosecutor is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but when quoting that statement, it says, in that paragraph, that Territorial Defence had 380 disarmed Croat police on the list, not that they disarmed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. You can see that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't see that because that's not what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at page 6 of your statement, the one that you gave to the Prosecutor in 1999? And in the second paragraph, could you read the third sentence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, but these are just excerpts from my statement. I haven't got my entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These are excerpts that the OTP provided to us and then we photocopied it and gave it to you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's just excerpts. I haven't got my proper statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We disclosed the proper statement and yesterday the witness had the statement. I think he has the statement from 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Yesterday, again, I had only these excerpts. I didn't have it yesterday either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you have a piece of paper before you that says, "The International Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons," and the number that you have is on that page is the last number 120?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That text has a stamp of the International Tribunal in the bottom right-hand corner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So please look at that page, or rather that text, please go up to page 6. The last digits are 125. That's the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher kindly show me the document? I gave the same statement to the witness yesterday. Could I just see whether the pages are mixed up or something? Your Honour, indeed, I gave the witness an incomplete text, a few pages are missing. I probably got the pages mixed up while bringing them in. I would kindly ask my learned friend of the Prosecution to help me if she has a proper copy of that statement. It would be important. It would be important because the witness is saying that it's not his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I've asked you to look at the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor on the 22nd of August 1999. Could you please look at the page that has in the upper right-hand corner a number ending with digits 125, and also it has number 00913301 underneath that. The text reads as follows. "The Territorial Defence of Bosanski Novi disarmed 380 Croatian policemen, according to a list." So there should have been 380 short-barrelled and long-barrelled guns. Then you say that this was not found in the warehouse. Is that what is written in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to -- it says, in English version, which was taken by the investigator, that Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence had 380 disarmed Croat police on the list. So there should have been 380 long- and short-barrelled weapons. So the original version doesn't say that TO disarmed but the TO had them on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can see the difference, Ms. Richterova. The question is -- I don't know now whether the person who translated the statement of the witness made a mistake or, I don't know. I think the witness will have to explain what the difference is. You see the problem, Mr. Milovancevic? What you have just read out to the witness, I'm sure in B/C/S, is different from what is in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I'm going to put this difference to the witness and I'm going to ask him whether what it says in B/C/S is what he stated to the OTP or not. I'm going to remind the witness that the complete text that refers to these 3830 Croatian policemen reads as follows, "The termed of Bosanski Novi disarmed 380 Croatian policemen according to the list, so there should have been 380 pieces of long-barrelled and short-barrelled weapons. Only five or six pistols and 12 or 13 rifles were handed over to the TO warehouse."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the question is, is this the statement that the witness gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the surrender of these members of the MUP, I probably did say this sentence, but in fact nobody took weapons from these people. But they themselves when they crossed over the bridge they threw them on a pile. So ordinary citizens of Serb ethnicity took these weapons from the pile. And I know of these personal searches and when these people were being brought in. That was done by the members headed by Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You know that because somebody told you about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned yesterday who it was, who said that to me, and I was present myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, on page 6 and yesterday when responding to the Prosecutor on the basis of page 6 of your statement from 1999, reference was made to the breakdown of the command structure of the police, but on page 5 of your statement, the text starts as follows: "The police split up in Bosanska Krupa and Hrvatska Kostajnica." What police are you referring to and what split-up are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how this happened in Hrvatska Kostajnica. I know that there was a split in the police in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is probably in context. Hrvatska Kostajnica fell on that same day when the delegation of the republic trade unions was travelling back so it was probably on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this same page, 5, of your statement, when you talk about the situation with the police in Bosanski Novi, you say that there was -- you say that there was a breakdown in the command structure of the police. Opposite orders came from the republic and from Banja Luka." Could you please explain this to us when orders are coming from the republic and when orders are coming from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite simple to explain. The dispatches that came from the then-republican MUP were not binding on anyone according to Stojan Zupljanin who was chief of the public security in Banja Luka. So orders came from Zupljanin and later the so-called MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about receiving contrary orders, did I understand you properly when you say -- that you're actually saying that you got one set of orders from Sarajevo and the different orders arrived from the Secretariat of the Interior in Banja Luka? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. But in Banja Luka it was the security centre which at that time was subordinated and it was also an integral part of the republican MUP or SUP rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that after the death of Mr. Umicevic, Dejan Samara became chief of police and that his task was either to divide the police or to force everyone to wear Serb insignia. That would be on page 6 of your statement to the OTP, the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the death of Mr. Umicevic, Stojan Zupljanin, as the head of the centre, appointed Dejan Samara active -- acting chief of the police station and every day he would see the top people of the SDS and others with whom Umicevic until then did not communicate at a personal level. While Dejan Samara was acting chief of the police station, a dispatch arrived. By then the MUP had officially been established of the Serb republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what it said. And an offer was made to all employees to sign an oath of loyalty. Authorised officials and people who worked there but were not authorised officials. Also insignia were supposed to be changed into tri-colours and also there was some kind of oath that had to be signed. I didn't sign it, and out of us Bosniaks in Bosanski Novi no one signed it and then we left that meeting after the dispatch was read out because we had refused to sign this oath and this solemn declaration. They said to us, "You can take your annual leave and then we'll see what will happen." But ultimately we ended up jobless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7 of this same statement of yours, in paragraph 3, you say that you had a meeting with Dzafer Kapetanovic, member of the main board of the SDA. And that you were asked it sign an oath of loyalty and go back to work, just to preserve the peace in town. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did state that. As we left the police station, the tensions went up even further, and people of Muslim Bosniak ethnicity felt even more threatened. In that sense, Mr. Dzafer Kapetanovic, who was killed during the war, insisted and asked us to come back to work, saying that this was in the interest of all citizens especially the Muslims to have their representatives in the police. However, even if we wanted to go back then, the then-chief probably had instructions from Banja Luka not to readmit us. He invited me to the hotel and we had a tete-a-tete meeting and discussed these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this period of time, had the referendum already been held on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia? In the first third of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I think it was, I know it was, because together with my colleagues, I was securing the polling stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by the late Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, on the 4th of April 1992, issued a conclusion about mobilising a Territorial Defence units and their subordination to public security stations in the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. And even if it was so, this information could not have reached us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but yesterday during my examination-in-chief, I covered only the new issue was the presence of Martic's police in Bosanski Novi. This goes well beyond these new issues which were raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only tried to get a response, or rather to ask the witness in order to check whether what he said is correct, that this was an attempt to create a Serb police or some sort of a Martic's Police under leadership of the SDS in a situation where, at the same time, a Bosnian Muslim police was being created from members of the Territorial Defence, in the same time period. The witness is referring to a time period in March-April and even May 1992, when war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but his testimony, whether written or oral, does not reflect that. So the picture it provides about the situation on the ground is completely warped, distorted. I would like a chance to ask the witness about the activity of the police in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the relevant time period because this is all in the same context as the activities of the so-called Martic's Police on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The situation, Your Honour, by your leave, just let me conclude my sentence, please, much more complex than a Red Beret. It is an extremely complex subject matter and there are many facts that have been glossed over here, although they do exist in the documentation, in the possession of the OTP. The Prosecutor has broadened his examination only to the extent that was convenient to the Prosecution, but to point this out, I do have to ask questions about the police. I have only two or three further questions about that and then I will have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this Bench doesn't make the laws. I know that the order was made that your cross-examination is limited to the Red Berets. And yesterday, leave was granted to you to cross-examine the witness on issues raised by the Prosecutor which were not already contained in the statement of the witness that had been given to you. What you are now saying is a completely new point. You are now telling me, this Bench, that you want to cross-examine on issues beyond what you are allowed to cross-examine because those issues had been glossed over. Shouldn't that -- shouldn't that have been mentioned and raised at the time before the order was made that you will be restricted to cross-examining on Red Berets only? You should have made the point then that you want to cross-examine on every point because things have been glossed over. I do not think this is the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand you, Your Honour. When we were providing the agreement to this, the examination had not yet taken place, which has changed the character of this witness's testimony. So, because the Prosecutor has broken the rules, we are now in a position where we are open to the objections Your Honours can rightly raise. The Prosecutor put questions falling beyond the scope of the witness statement and they alter the essence of the statement, not just particular facts, but the entire context, which is very important. I will, however, abide by Your Honour's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have a question for you, Witness. In the time period when you say the condition for remaining in the police was the signing of a statement of loyalty, did the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina issue a decision on the 29th of April - and this will be my last question - about the blocking of all roads in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all military facilities of the JNA, and preventing the JNA from coming out of its barracks on the fast planning and use of combat means in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was signed by Hasan Efendic, who was the commander, the military commander, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say nothing about this decision because it was not available to me. I was in Bosanski Novi until the 8th of May when I fled -- 1992, when I fled Bosanski Novi with my family. After I stopped working in the police force, I no longer had access to dispatches and information, but I doubt that they could have reached Bosanski Novi because they had to be filtered through Banja Luka. I really don't know about this. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And my last question to you in the cross-examination is the following: First, do you know who Vitomir Zepinic is? Was he the Deputy Minister of Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Avdo Hebib, and was he the assistant Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And do you know that acting on orders from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 11th of July 1991, they toured the municipalities of Banja Luka, Bosanska Gradiska, Bosanska Dubica, and Bosanski Novi, and compiled detailed written information for the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they say that the major party to blame for the situation is the aggressive military action of members of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, their incursions into the territory of Bosanski Novi, the crossings of small groups of members of the MUP in uniform on to Bosnian territory, incursions by special-purpose policemen, disseminating fear among citizens of Serb and Muslim ethnicity, and causing them to arm themselves? I know my question is very long, but I'm asking you whether you are aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Vito Zepinic personally and Mr. Avdo Hebib also. I am not aware of this information, and I doubt that this kind of information existed. It's true that in Bosanski Novi or rather in the village of Ravnice, two members of the MUP swam across the river Una. One of them was called Landeka. That was his last name, and he was brought into the police station. I was there when that happened. These two men were taken away by the military police to the investigative prison, detention unit, in Banja Luka. As for any large-scale crossings of any members of the MUP in the territory of Bosanski Novi, I have never seen or heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And my last question to you is: Do you want to say that the official information of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 11th of July 1991, bearing the stamp and SAO 2-0639, that this information is untrue and incorrect? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived and worked in Bosanski Novi municipality, and I know for certain that although there may have been shelling in parts of Bosanska Kostajnica, where, on Bajo hill, on our side there were mortars, guns and so on, it's possible that there was an exchange of fire across the river Una there. But as for Bosanski Novi and the area around Bosanski Novi, I assert under full liability that there were no crossings by Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Any re-examination, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have only one short question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Bosnian population, Muslim population, in the municipality of Bosanski Novi in 1992? Did they stay in that municipality or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Bosanski Novi at the time because, as I said, I left on the 8th of May, but I do know that during the summer of 1992, the male civilian population was arrested in their homes and taken to the Mlakve stadium where they were held for a few days. There was the first official camp in Bosnia-Herzegovina, detention camp. After that, the population was moved out under the escort of the United Nations, between 10 and 12 inhabitants in one day of Bosanski Novi municipality, counting, of course, women and children. Part --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object. This redirect has nothing to do with the cross-examination or the content of the statement provided by the witness to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, the -- Mr. Milovancevic was asking about Serbs coming to Bosanski Novi, so I'm asking what happened to people from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was about what happened to the Serbs, whether Serbs arrived from Croatia. However, the Prosecutor is asking about the Muslim population and that is a broadening of the topic that I raised during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor ask about the Muslim population or did she ask about the civilian population of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I asked what happened to the Bosnian Muslim population in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, to respond to my learned friend, during my cross-examination, I asked the witness about the civilian population from the neighbouring republic of Croatia, the Serb population fleeing from Croatia into Bosanski Novi. This is an entirely different topic that has nothing to do with the questions I put to the witness during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question would be where this population went, and we would know where they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which one, the population --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The civilian population of Bosnian ethnicity, Muslim ethnicity. But if I -- I am in your hands. If you don't allow this question, I won't ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't seem like it arises from the cross-examination, Ms. Richterova. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask two questions, Mr. Krupic? First, getting back to this issue of mobilisation in 1991, or 1990 and 1991, did you say that Muslims also would show up for this call-up but were sent back, in fact? Was this before Izetbegovic made this recommendation or also after, if I got it right? Could you explain that a little once more?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991, when the war broke out in Croatia, there was a general mobilisation valid for everyone, of all ethnicities. The Muslim Bosniak population partially responded to this call-up. In every call-up paper, there was a time and place where the conscript had to report. When they reported, some of them were sent home straight away, and only a smaller number were sent to the war front. After the public speech of Mr. Izetbegovic, who said that there was no duty to respond to the call-up, he didn't say Muslims or Serbs, he said nobody had to respond to the call-up. After that, 99 per cent of the Muslims no longer responded to these call-ups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then another question. You referred to a group with the name Suha Rebra. Do you remember that? Can you explain what this term means, where this expression came from?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a group of underage young men who broke into huts that were used for curing meat in the neighbourhood, and the word suha rebra means spare ribs. That's how they got their name because they used to steal spare ribs and other cured meat from these curing huts, and they were hooligans, juvenile delinquents when they were young men, and they got this nickname and now they had grown up and this was a large group of men, 40 or 50 strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I thought that has something to do with some food, and this was the origin, in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, you said in your statement of the 22nd of August 1999, that there were check-points on the bridges between Bosanska and Hrvatska Kostajnica and between Bosanski Nova and Dvor and those check-points were to keep reservists coming into town carrying weapons and combat equipment. What ethnicity -- what ethnic group would these reserves have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you went on to -- you went on to speak about reservists that came into town with weapons, wearing kokardas, and Chetnik insignia. What would kokarda be now?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A kokarda is a Chetnik insignia. My former, I didn't know what it was either so I asked my former colleagues. There are these insignia with skulls and then there are some that go back to the days of some King Petar, or whoever, I don't know. I was born after that but I know that the association is the Chetniks from the Second World War. So it's metal insignia worn on caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are they associated with any particular group or --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever wanted to, wore them, I assume because not everybody wore those kokardas either. Some people were pleased to be called Chetniks, whereas others were offended if they were called Chetniks. It depended on one's own personal feelings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Krupic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of February 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I pick up from the questions of Judge Nosworthy about these spare ribs? Who were they subordinated to, the Suha Rebra?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suha Rebra primarily worked for themselves and for their own interest because it involved looting primarily, and I assume, and claim, rather, that all the dirty work that was supposed to be done was done for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have referred to the chief of the Bosanski Novi police, Mr. Umicevic. Just for the sake of clarity, can you spell his name? I see at two places in your two different statements, the name is spelled differently.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuro Umicevic. I also noticed that in several places it said, "Umicevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it's a U at the beginning, not an O?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, it's a U.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I am very slow to understand when people are talking in court here so I'm going to ask you questions which you may very well have answered already. I'm going to ask you to bear with me. How many towns or villages or communities were attacked that you testified about in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attacked during the war in Bosanski Novi, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Was Bosanski Novi attacked? And if so, were there also other areas outside Bosanski Novi which were attacked?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I think the 11th of May it was, the armed attack started against the Muslim Bosniak population in Bosanski Novi. On that occasion, Urije and Prevosavlje and part of Vidovije were shelled, and these are neighbourhoods populated by Bosniaks only. And also the so-called Dolina Japra. That is Blagaj, Japra, Suhaca, Hozici, and Alici, are areas where Bosniak Muslims lived and they were shelled. And on that occasion several people were killed. Men, women and children. And all were expelled from that area to Blagaj, and from there they were deported on trains in train cars for livestock towards Ozren and they were detained at a stadium and then they were moved out under the escort of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, these areas that you have mentioned are all areas within the area -- within the district of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You talk of Bosniaks. What are Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks are the former Muslims. As a rule nobody asked me whether I wanted to be a Bosniak or not. I would be happiest to call myself a Bosnian of the Islamic faith. However there was not a referendum on this. A decision was passed at state level that the former Muslims will be linked to the name of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and would be called Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is meant by former Muslims? Have these people stopped being Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially, they are Bosniaks of the Muslim faith or rather the Islamic faith. Just like Serbs are Orthodox Christians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you also referred, when you dealt with the population of Bosanski Novi, you referred to Yugoslavs. Who are Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavs were people who felt that their affiliation was with the state of Yugoslavia. For the most part Yugoslavs were people who had mixed marriages, and when I say mixed marriages, I mean the following: If the wife was a Bosniak or Muslim and the husband a Serb or a Croat, and the other way around. So they were mainly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness says "Muslims."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, of course, people who felt that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Outside Bosanski Novi, or before we leave Bosanski Novi, you said that the population was removed by the United Nations to Ozren, is that it? No, no. Yes. What finally happened to this population? Did it finally come back to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the population from the so-called Japra valley, Japra Blagaj, Suhaca, Hozici, they were all deported in trains and cattle train cars, and then when they were returned two or three days later, then a convoy was organised under the escort of the UN and once they left from Bosanski Novi and they were returned and the other time they managed to leave in organised fashion, to get to the territory of Croatia, and then they moved to different western countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that as we speak, they are not in Bosanski Novi? They have gone to different western countries?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi, according to some of the pre-war estimates, had between 14 and 17.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "70.000"] Muslims, called Bosniaks nowadays. I claim with full responsibility that in Bosanski Novi now there aren't even 5.000 left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think there is a mistake in the transcript. It should read 17, not 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Between 14 and 17. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I understood 40 and 70.000 -- 14 and 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you clear that up? Can you give us that population again? You say --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 14 -- from 14 to 17.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 14 to 17.000. Thank you very much. Okay. What was the extent, if you know, of the damage of property in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to talk about damage, very hard. The damage is enormous. After all, the areas that were not populated, Suhaca, Hozici, Alici, not a single house remained intact. They were demolished, destroyed. And these people were employed abroad, in Germany, Switzerland, Austria, et cetera. So these were the richest people in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Machines, tractors, remained behind, trucks and so on and so forth in addition to the houses that were equipped. Now, Blagaj Rijeka, Blagaj Japra, places that were populated, that is in Bosanski Novi, the facilities were mainly -- are mainly still there, the houses are still there, but there is no furniture or anything else that was inside the houses to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What happened to that furniture that used to be inside the houses?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part that furniture was stolen by people. People took it all for themselves, from the neighbouring Serb villages they came with tractors and trucks and just took this away, and allegedly, the then-army took part of it into some warehouse and then distributed it. For example I know about my own apartment that remained furnished. I did not even take my family photographs from the apartment. My former colleagues entered my apartment and, when we spoke on the telephone, they asked me whether they could take the TV set, the video, et cetera, I gave up on this altogether. So I know where all these things are, but now I'm not interested in this and I'm not interested in the appliances, furniture, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Krupic, and I understand that this probably evokes certain emotions in you, but we are not talking about you personally here. We are talking about the entire community of Bosanski Novi. Are you able to tell, in numbers, the number of people who might have been killed during this attack? I'm talking about civilians, not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When these Bosniak villages were attacked, I'm sure that dozens of civilians were killed. I couldn't give you an accurate number but it certainly wasn't less than 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these 50 who would have been killed, would they have been armed at the time of being killed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I claim with full responsibility that none of them had been armed, and in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, not a single bullet was fired by the Bosniak Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Outside Bosanski Novi, but in the same region, were there any other areas that were similarly attacked?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, attacks were carried out in all areas, including Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, but Bosanski Novi, I think, in relation to the other municipalities, fared much better and involved less victims. Of course, any victim is important, but Mr. Izet Muhamedic came to lead the SDA then, and he and they asked the population not to put up any kind of resistance and not to go into any kind of armed conflicts with the other side. In that case, there probably would have been many, many more victims, many, many more casualties, whereas in Sanski Most and Kljuc, the situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the extent of deaths in those areas, in Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you any figures, but there were many, many more than in Bosanski Novi. If you look at the other municipalities, Bosanski Novi has much, much less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In terms of property in those areas, what would you say the extent of destruction was, if there was any destruction?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that complete villages were destroyed, which, in fact, did not even exist any longer until 1995. That is when the population started returning there and now these population -- these villages are populated to a certain extent, not to the extent to which they were populated in 1992, though. But people are returning to their houses and to their property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You referred yesterday to the fall of Hrvatska Kostajnica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the extent of the damage in that area?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with my colleague --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One evening I went to carry out an on-site inspection -- investigation in Hrvatska Kostajnica, where there was a classic murder, because after these wartime events, Hrvatska Kostajnica was in bad shape. It was night, to be sure, but I could see that it was very badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to -- would you say the entire city was flattened or just give us an estimation of the extent of the damage?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there had been shelling. You can't say that the entire town was destroyed but there was damage in many places in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the number of deaths in Hrvatska Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because it's in another state, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also referred yesterday to the looting of Bosanska Kostajnica. Remember that? At the time when Bosanska Kostajnica surrendered, if I remember your evidence correctly. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. For a time I was present. When I was talking about the robbery, I was referring to watches, jewellery and so on, by Martic's unit, which was assigned to search those men who had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. So it was the search of individuals, it was not the area that was being attacked? Sorry, we've gone far beyond time for break off. We should have broken off at 20 past ten. I didn't realise that. This may be a convenient time to stop. We'll come back at 10 to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, let me just get clarity on this last point that we were dealing with before we went out for the break. You say Bosanska Kostajnica was looted. Am I right that you said that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Bosanska Kostajnica was looted but that the people who surrendered there, and they were policemen of the Republic of Croatia, that they were robbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there was no attack on it.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, there probably was, but it's about 30 kilometres away from Bosanski Novi, so I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much. Any questions arising, Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the question put to you about the meaning of the word kokarda and who wore it, you gave an explanation. The question is as follows: Do you know that the kokarda was the insignia worn on the caps of members of the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and that this kokarda was worn by those members of the royal army who did not recognise the German occupation, who were monarchists and anticommunists, and who, through most of the period of World War II, enjoyed the support of London and Washington? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to a former colleague of mine about the kokarda. He knew more about it than I did. He was a Serb and he was older than me. There were two kinds of kokardas worn during the previous war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was the kokarda associated with the kingdom, the former kingdom and the insignia of that army, and there was another kind of kokarda with a skull. That was the so-called Chetnik kokarda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The colleague you spoke to, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in 1950. His father and his mother had participated in World War II and he was a work colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering His Honour's questions, you said, speaking of the victims among the civilian population on the territory of Bosanski Novi, that you assert with full responsibility that not a single bullet was fired by the Bosniak people. Can you tell us what happened to the weapons carried by SDA units, the red fezzes and the weapons that Hasim Valjevac and others distributed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again: I assert with full responsibility that on the territory of Bosanski Novi municipality, not a single bullet was fired during the war by the Bosniak side. As for some sort of red fezzes, there is the first time I've heard of them. It's true that fezzes are red in colour but that there were groups wearing red fezzes, I don't know that. And as for Valjevac, I don't know what you said his name was, this man who allegedly distributed weapons. Could you repeat his last name, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Hasim Valjevac?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasim Valjevac is from Bosanska Kostajnica, he was employed in the Bosanski Novi municipality. I think he now works in the Kostajnica municipality. And about Hasim Valjevac having some sort of red fezzes, well, those are just tales for small children, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are the Green Berets tales for small children?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could buy any colour beret, green, red, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering the Benches questions about the situation in Hrvatska Kostajnica, you said that one night you saw what the situation there was because you were carrying out an on-site investigation, and this was a different state, as you say, so how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague, Esad Brkic, who was a crime technician, a forensic technician, was asked to go there and photograph the crime scene of a murder that had taken place in a private apartment, and I went there with him. I accompanied him. They did not have a forensic technician there in Hrvatska Kostajnica, when the Serb forces took over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who was it, then, who invited you to go and help, the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian police from Hrvatska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And you cooperated with them normally?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the active police from Dvor Na Uni and Hrvatska Kostajnica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Answering the Bench's questions as to the kind of damage there was in Hrvatska Kostajnica, you said that you were there at night-time, that you did see some damage, as it was night-time, how was it possible for you to tell which house belonged to whom, which houses were Serb, which were Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my response, I mentioned neither Croat nor Serb nor Muslim houses. All I said was that there was damage from shelling, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there Serb, Croat and Muslim houses in Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another question for you. When answering the questions from the Bench about the damage that happened during the war, you mentioned Bosanski Novi and other places. From the information you gave, answering the questions by the Prosecutor, you said you hadn't been in Bosanski Novi. I assume you hadn't been in all those other places during the war. Did you talk to the people from those places and did you get your information about the damage from them? And everything else that happened?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not exactly because what he said he was there after the war, and it was in his statement. It's not what he answered to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put to the witness that he himself said that in May 1992, he left Bosanski Novi, so he was not in Bosanski Novi, he was somewhere else. As he spoke of a number of other villages, I asked him where he got his information. The essence of my question was: Did he talk about the casualties and the damage that occurred during the war with people from those places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you want to know, I will tell you. Towards the end of 1995, and in 1996, every month or every fortnight after the end of the war, I did go to Bosanski Novi. I still visit Bosanski Novi often. I have friends there, colleagues. Furthermore, if you want to know where I got this information, I won't keep silent about the following. During the war I was the chief of the crime police of the Banja Luka police centre in exile in Travnik. We took statements about genocide, about crimes, and delivered all this to the Ministry of the Interior of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another question for you. You said you took statements from people and you mentioned the damage that occurred. In your statement to the Prosecution, did you say, "On one occasion, after the beginning of the war, I happened to meet some people from Bosanski Novi. They were all of the same opinion, that their problems had been caused by their own politicians and the West? Ordinary people had to take sides in the first few days, either to take the side of the party or to be considered opponents and therefore enemies." Did you say that on page 7 of your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Krupic, thank you so much for coming to testify. We are finished with your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but the witness started answering the question, and he was not allowed to finish the question. He was just -- "Yes, I did. And there is --" and Mr. Milovancevic just interrupted him so we don't know what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to finish, complete that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me. Your Honour, my question, which I put to the witness, was whether he had spoken to people, and whether he said in his statement is what he was told by those people. His answer was "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to continue but you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this answer is sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please finish your answer, Mr. Krupic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that, and I only wish to add that those who were not following the party line were immediately -- was immediately branded a traitor of the Serb people. There is a saying, "He who is not with us is against us." But it doesn't have to be that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krupic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, once again, thank you so much. I'm sorry about that little misunderstanding. You are excused, as I said. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before calling the next witness, just one little point I want to raise with -- can we please move into private session for purposes of what I want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't want to hear what we are going to say in private?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before we begin, I want to explain to you various protective measures which have been granted to you for purposes of your testimony in this proceeding. You have been granted face distortion, which means that your face will be distorted in any broadcast of public portions of this proceeding. You've been granted a pseudonym, which means that you will be referred to only by your pseudonym and not by your true name. You've also been granted voice distortion which means that your voice will be distorted during any broadcasts of public portions of this proceeding. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition, in order to protect your identity, whenever we discuss topics which could tend to disclose your identity, could identify you, we will do those in private session. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That means that when we are in public session, I'm going to ask you to please take care to avoid -- I've been leaving my microphone on -- to avoid using your name or referring to anything that could identify you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'm going to show you what we refer to as a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there a matter that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are being asked to speak a little up. They can't pick your voice up, those who have to interpret what you're saying. Speak a bit louder. Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at this document and do not read out what it says out loud but please tell me if that is your name that appears on the document? And having just seen this moments before you came in, I'm a little concerned that maybe your name is misspelled, and if it is, could you take a pen and write the correct spelling above your name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the usher show the document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I say it out loud or should I just write out what is correct here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You should write out what is correct. Please do not say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the usher could bring it back to me and then I'll ask that it be shown to the Defence and to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for misspelling your name.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right. It's just a question of spelling. It's all right. It's just a question of spelling. That's the only mistake that was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that document be admitted into evidence and placed under seal, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document showing the witness's correct name is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 281, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Witness, you will be referred to in these proceedings by your pseudonym, MM-079, or alternatively as just, "Witness." Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I think what His Honour Judge Moloto was about to tell you is that the microphone won't pick up you nodding your head or shaking your head. You always have to answer the question verbally. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best and try to take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'll also remind you again that you're going to have to, I think, speak a little bit louder because it's very difficult for the interpreters. A the voice distortion is very good and you won't -- if you speak louder, you won't break through the voice distortion. There is nothing to be concerned about. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I tried to distort my voice in any way. It's just the way I speak naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. If you could just try to remember to speak up a little bit it would be of great assistance to all of us, particularly the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you for some background questions about the federal Ministry of the Interior. Could you tell us first of all the two parts of the federal Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- well, I wouldn't call it two parts. Two departments or two sections. The public security and the state security sector. These sectors existed at every level in the republics, and lower level municipal and regional organisations of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the -- can you tell us what -- by what abbreviation the public security sector was known and what -- and by what abbreviation the state security sector was known?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviations were used as follows: SDB for the State Security Service, and SJB for the Public Security Service. This may have differed from republic to republic. However, the first letter of every word was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the last sentence of your answer. Maybe it's a translation issue. You said, "However, the first letter of every word was taken." Oh, I understand. It's an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, a little slow. Now, the -- I was just going to ask you if there was a similar organisation in the republic ministries of Interior and you started to answer that. Could you explain for example by giving -- by referring to the Republic of Serbia, was it organised in the same way with the same two sectors, the SJB and the SDB?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In almost every republic or rather in every republic, there were two services at the Ministry of Interior, the Public Security Service and the State Security Service. Their organisation within these services, depending on each republic, had administrations. For example, the first administration of the SDB, if it existed in Serbia, for example, would be called the third or the second administration in another republic. It would all depend on the difficulty of the work that the republic in question felt was at issue for that republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Staying at the level of the two different sectors, the Public Security Service and the State Security Service, can you tell us, in general terms, and briefly, what the different roles were of the State Security Service and the Public Security Service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the name itself shows, the State Security Service had the task of protecting the legal and social order in the country. It dealt with political crime, terrorism, extremism, and intelligence work. Whereas the Public Security Service dealt with ordinary crime. For example, traffic, drugs, economic crime, theft, robbery and so on. Those were their duties. This was general crime, such as exists in every country in the world and has organisations to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And I think this is clear but just to be absolutely clear, there was existed a federal Ministry of Interior with these two sectors, Public Security Service and State Security Service, and in each republic there existed a republican Ministry of Interior and -- with these two sectors, the Public Security Service and the State Security Service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, up until 1988, what was the relationship between the federal State Security Service or the federal DB and the DBs or state security services of the various republics?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1988, the federal service controlled the republican services, so there was subordinate-superior relationship with all the six republics and the two autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would employees of the federal -- I'm sorry, of the republican services ever go to work for the federal service?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, whether they were working for the federal services. They were working for the services of their own republics. But they were duty bound to coordinate their work with the of the federal service, to ask for guidelines and instructions from the federal service. Every contact among the republics or the ministries of the various republics, took place either in cooperation with or through the federal ministry. We were the coordinators between the republics and a link between the services in the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would there be -- before 1988 would there be sharing of information between the federal service and the republican services?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was quite usual and it was according to the rules of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I've been asking about the time period before 1988. Did something happen in 1988 that changed this?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a difference in the period before 1988 and after 1988, or 1989. Until the political conflicts that occurred on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, both at the head of the League of Communists, which fell apart, as did the Communist Parties of Yugoslavia, and this was immediately reflected in the work of the services of the various republics. In their attitude toward the federal organs, I can only refer to my own service. The various republics began to withhold information. Coordination and work with the federal Ministry of the Interior and the federal State Security Service, well, this started in Slovenia and Croatia, and all this was reflected on the work of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did changes occur in the federal ministry, in particular in the State Security Service, at this time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, individual republics, Slovenia, Croatia, later on Bosnia, then Macedonia, began withholding certain information and rather than asking us for assistance, guidelines, coordination, instructions, well, this was later, also transferred to other republics, this did not happen all of a sudden. It went on until 1992. It progressed, this separation of the republics. It depended on each republic and the time it separated in. But you could feel this in the way work was coordinated, in the correspondence and also as regarded personnel because various republics stopped sending staff to work in the federal services, at least as far as operations went. It was only in formal terms that cooperation continued. The presence of Slovenia or Croatia was only formal. It was different than it had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When these republics started -- stopped sending staff to work in the federal services, who took their places?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in the federal ministry started becoming scattered from that year onwards. The people left. The only people who remained were those who had family ties or other ties to Belgrade. Those whose links to Belgrade were purely professional went back to their own republics. Staff members from Serbia, of course, remained. There were some employees from other republics who remained working there until 1992, and then they had to leave too because they lost their jobs. Of course, due to this staff shortage, the ministry of the Republic of Serbia sent us people to fill the vacancies, but it was really a formality because we had staff members but we didn't have any work, because the other republics stopped sending us information and without their information we couldn't do our jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that last answer, you said that "Staff members who were from Serbia, of course, remained." Why is that "of course"? Why did they remain?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that those who had families in Belgrade or came from Serbia had to stay in Serbia, but those who had only been sent from various republics to do a job, they lost their jobs and then they went back to their home republics, whereas staff members from Serbia had not only professional but also family links in Belgrade and that's why they stayed. Well, one might say that Serbia was gradually taking over certain functions, and when the functions of the autonomous provinces ceased to exist, Serbia gradually began taking over the work of the federal institutions, especially the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
