utterances.text: In 1989, who became the federal Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1989, after the departure of Culafic, we were left without a minister for a time, and then Petar Gracanin a retired general of the Yugoslav army arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what year he arrived? Was it in 1989 or was it later?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1989, but please don't hold me to it, because quite a long time has elapsed. I think it was maybe in September 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall until when he served, what year he stopped serving as the federal Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the federal minister until 1992. Whether it was February or March, I'm not sure, 1992, but, again, please don't hold me to the precise date. It could have been a month before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. For this purpose, the precise date is not important. Can you tell us, if you know, how did he become the federal Minister of Interior? That is, was he promoted by anybody or --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not be promoted any higher because he was a general and a national hero. It was more a duty and a task that he had to do. It wasn't a promotion for him, because you can't get higher than a general, or you couldn't in the then-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was using the word in a different sense to mean -- did anybody advocate him becoming, to your knowledge, advocate him becoming the Minister of Interior? Did anybody support him or how did he become the Minister of Interior, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he was appointed, my colleagues and I commented on it. We commented on his arrival as Minister of the Interior because we felt that he was too old. He had been in a war where he had been wounded more than once, and that he was not up to the challenges of the job he had taken up. Those were the comments we made among ourselves. And we thought he had been appointed by Serbia, that he had been appointed Minister of the Interior in order to carry out a certain task. I can give you an example. Almost all the previous ministers starting from Herljevic who was a military man before he became Minister of the Interior, Culafic was the only civilian the only one who had been a politician actually, but it was the practice in earlier periods to appoint generals as ministers of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are about to take a break but before we take the break, let me ask you this question. When you say you thought he was appointed by Serbia, did you think he was appointed or advocated by any particular person in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he was a Serb cadre, he was an ethnic Serb, he came from Serbia, he lived in Belgrade, probably he was involved in political life, the political life of Serbia, that is, and two Macedonians had been nominated and one from Slovenia, but as they didn't want to send them to Serbia, Serbia came in to fill the gap because most probably it was the Serb leaders who were in power at the time who appointed him as Minister of the Interior. He was appointed not elected, because I think that had he been elected in the -- according to the proper procedure, he would have had to be someone from Macedonia. That was the kind of rota system there was. But Macedonia was beginning to withhold its staff members from the federal services, although there were still some staff members from Macedonia and other republics. But when Gracanin was appointed, this was an attempt to solve that problem because the Ministry of the Interior was in Serbia and that activity was felt there more than in other republics. So most probably Gracanin was appointed by the top leadership. There was already political turbulence within Serbia and in the League of Communists. Gracanin was probably close to the leading people, those headed by the late Mr. Milosevic, and the choice fell on him, and he appointed Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that this would be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at 20 to 1. Please be back at 20 to 1. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did the Croatian authorities tell you anything about what was happening at that time in Knin and in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Deputy Minister of the Interior of Croatia said that the biggest problem in Croatia was in the Krajina area, around Knin, Benkovac and Obrovac, the so-called SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, can I ask a question? When we are in open session, don't we lift the blind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because for one thing there is actually nobody back there. It's as a precaution, but if there was a public -- the public was there, then if we lifted the blind they would be able to see the witness and he would be identified. In other courtrooms, and I think you'll see this next week, the public sits behind the witness and the way it's done is there is a screen put around the witness so that there can be a public there and watching the session without seeing who the witness is. But the way this courtroom is configured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the Croatian authorities said that the biggest problem in Croatia was the Krajina area, the so-called SAO Krajina. Did they tell you what kind of problems they were having, what the issues were?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then assistant Minister of Croatia said that in their terms the OUP in Knin, that is to say the police in Knin, had separated, that it was no longer under the jurisdiction of the Croatian state and Croatian law, that it carried out some kind of organisation or reorganisation of its own in the area of Knin, Benkovac, and Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- did they say who had initiated or caused this reorganisation that they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned Milan Martic then as one of the protagonists of all of these actions, which -- who had declared himself as, as he put it then, secretary of the Secretariat of the SUP in Knin, who placed the entire police under his own control, his own authority, that part of the police that consisted of members of the Croatian ethnic group were dismissed, as they said, from the ranks of the police of the Secretariat in Knin, that he admitted quite a few of his own people into the police, with Serb ethnic backgrounds, and that he was operating under some laws that were not in force in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Then there was also reference to the putting up of roadblocks and the participation of the police from SAO Krajina under Martic's leadership in this. The roadblocks were placed as protection for Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian authorities say anything about Milan Martic's relationship, if any, to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said then, or rather the assistant minister said then, that several times they tried to establish contact with Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they say why they were trying to establish contact with Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to recommend to him to abide by Croatian law and the rules and regulations of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior. In return, they said that they had offered him the top job in the police in Knin. However, as the assistant minister said then, Martic did not accept that. His only wish was for him to establish a Secretariat of the Interior in the territory of Knin and other organs in the territory of Benkovac and Obrovac, in order to keep all power in SAO Krajina in the hands of the then-government or the then-leadership of the SAO Krajina in that area and all control over the work of the Ministry of the Interior, to keep it under his own control. The assistant Minister of Croatia also said that Martic was doing all of that as persuaded by Belgrade, that that was not his own doing, but that he fell under the influence of Belgrade and the Belgrade structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that they told you that Milan Martic was admitting quite a few of his own people into the police with Serb ethnic backgrounds. Did they tell you anything about how or where these people were trained?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister or rather the assistant Minister of Croatia in the Ministry of the Interior said nothing about that, because that meeting was practically a preliminary meeting. Everything was being said in general terms. Nothing was said in concrete terms. It was left for us to clarify it through our future work. That is to say manning the services, the organisation of jurisdiction, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about the training of people who were being admitted into the police with Serb ethnic backgrounds later on, in other meetings or through other means?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on we found out in contacts with the other members of the Ministry of the Interior in the area of the SAO Krajina, and in contact with ordinary citizens of either ethnic background, that these new personnel who were admitted into the police, were being trained in a place called Golubic, not far away from Knin, that that is where there is this kind of training centre for members of the police of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about who did the training there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this information was not accessible to the ordinary citizens with whom we were in contact every day, it was mostly personnel from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. We unofficially talked to members of the police of Krajina. These were unofficial operative contacts so that we could learn something. Later on, the group itself established that these were cadres from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn what Milan Martic's role was with respect to the training camp at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically we did not learn anything, but according to the hierarchy, Milan Martic had to take all initiatives in terms of the number of cadres, how many people would be taken in, how they would be trained, and what their function would be later in the territory of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you made some references to the organisation of the police, and you made a reference to -- you used the term OUP and you -- at another time you used the term SUP or SUP. Can you explain how the police was organised, if you know, if this is something you learned? How was the police organised in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia, and how did -- how was it changed by Milan Martic in the SAO Krajina? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And if it would be easier for you to make a diagram, we could do that. I could give you a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem whatsoever either, because this is a generally known thing. At least for us who lived down there. This structure was well known. The federal Ministry of the Interior was at the head of all these services. Then one step lower was the republican Ministry of the Interior. As for Serbia, there were two provincial ministries as well of the interior, of Kosovo and Vojvodina respectively, and then as for the other lines, it depended. Sometimes there would be slight variations in different republics because every republic had an organisation of its own but about 90 per cent would be similar or the same. In larger cities or larger towns, that covered a larger territory, there were Secretariats of the Interior. The lower level was the municipality and also smaller towns or villages, MUP, OUP, and in terms of all the duties they had to perform, their authority was less than at the higher level. And then there was the station of the police, the police station, as such. I'm talking about the level where I was present. Sometimes for example there would be a police station with a single policeman only. I don't know how clear I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think maybe it would be helpful if you could draw this in a diagram form, and if you could do it with respect to the area that we are talking about, that is Knin, Benkovac, Sibenik, and so forth, if you could draw the different levels at the time n the Republic of Croatia, and then if -- and then you could show us on the diagram how Milan Martic changed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if it could be put on the ELMO? And I suppose we have to switch to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a ballpoint pen, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And if you could start at the top with the republic SUP in the Republic of Croatia, and then show -- do the diagram from there. So the top should be the republic Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you read for us what it is you've written, starting from the top, on this piece of paper? I can see "RSUP"? What have you put --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the republican Secretariat of the Interior of a particular republic, in this case Croatia. Its headquarters was in Zagreb. At the lower level is the Secretariat of the Interior and those existed in every larger municipality in Croatia. For example, Sibenik and Zadar each had their own Secretariat, whereas Knin did not have one at the time. The Secretariats had a higher level of authority and obligation. For example, a Secretariat could issue a passport, a driving licence, a traffic licence, and so on. The lower level organ was the organ of the interior, and these were in smaller municipalities. They encompassed a smaller territory and had fewer personnel. They, in some places -- I can't be sure about Croatia -- but for the most part these organs could not issue passports, driving licences, traffic licences, and so on. There was within the competence of the Secretariat. However, the organ to issue a public -- an identity card and other documents valid for the citizens. Then there was a police department underneath that. They did not deal with general jobs such as could be done by the organ or the Secretariat. These were simply policemen covering a municipality or a local commune. Don't take my word for it, I don't know whether there were five, 10 or 20 people there, depending on the area they covered. And at the lowest level was a police station, which would be in a certain town or village. For example, if a train passed through a certain village or town, then there would also be a police station close to the railway station. And it was just a room basically, where policemen had a key and they could go there if necessary. It was more a place to go than an office. There would be two or three policemen patrolling the area. I'm not very familiar with it because I didn't work for that service, but I did initially, of course, but later on I was transferred, so I don't know how clear I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I want to just go through what the abbreviations are at each level. The top obviously, you've written R SUP, republic SUP. The next level, what is the abbreviation, what's the abbreviation for the next level?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And I believe you -- yeah, go ahead, why don't you write the abbreviations at each level?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And OUP. Then OM. And SM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that the -- at the SUP level was Sibenik and Zadar but not Knin. What level -- could you write "Sibenik and Zadar" just at that level, underneath the SUP there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And are there any examples of OMs that you can give us?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure about OMs, whether Benkovac and Obrovac had OMs, I think, according to what there was on the ground. I'm not sure. Because when we arrived there, they already had organs, but I visited Benkovac and Obrovac two or three times, and as far as I was able to see what the buildings looked like, most probably they were just police -- I apologise for sometime using the word Milicija and sometimes Policija, they both refer -- when I use them I'm referring to the same thing. I think that in Pakrac - I may be wrong - there may have been a police station there. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But from what you could observe when you visited Benkovac and Obrovac, did they appear to you to be at the level of the OUP or the OM or can you explain?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, when I was there, were at the level of the OUP. Before that, they had very small premises, and judging by those premises, they couldn't have done all the work that falls within the competence of an OUP. It looked more like a police station, the SM. If there was a reorganisation internally and they wanted to do various kinds of work in one and the same room, one and the same office, I don't know. I didn't go into all those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you've just made reference to the structure as it was when you were there, and you observed it and how it had been before. You've told us that Knin was an OUP. Was that how it was before or how it was in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, it was the Secretariat of the Interior of the SAO Krajina. Before that, as we had been informed by Mr. Vukosic and the assistant Minister of Croatia, Knin had been an OUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony correctly, within the structure in the Republic of Croatia, it's how you have drawn it. Sibenik and Zadar were SUPs and Knin was an OUP but when the SAO Krajina was created, Knin became -- Knin became a SUP?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It went a rung up the ladder so from being an organ it became a Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did the same thing happen with Benkovac and Obrovac? Did they move up the ladder whether the SAO Krajina was created?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the SAO Krajina was formed, and the Knin OUP became the Knin SUP, then automatically the Benkovac and Obrovac OUPs also increased their authority and competences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one minute, should that be the OMs instead of OUPs, in relation to Benkovac and Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Benkovac and Obrovac, before the SAO Krajina was formed, were OMs. After the SAO Krajina was formed, they became OUPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, finally on this chart, you testified earlier that the Croatian authorities told -- said that they had offered to make Milan Martic -- put him in charge of a SUP in Knin. Am I understanding your prior testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The minister told us they wanted to promote or, rather, strengthen the competencies of the OUP in Knin and to create a SUP there, because in the OUP he could have only been the chief of the OUP, not the secretary of the SUP. So that's a higher level post. That's what the deputy minister said, that they offered Martic, that they would organise a SUP in Knin and offer him the post of secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But the condition of that was that he would have to accept Croatian laws and Croatian jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Without that, they would not do it. The condition was for him to accept the legislation and laws of Croatia. There were also the procedures, the rules of procedure of the organ of the interior and he would have to accept the rules of procedure that were in force throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And just while we are on this topic, could you tell us again what did they tell you his response was to this offer that they were making to him?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said very decidedly that Martic refused to receive them, although they tried in various ways to establish contact with him, directly and indirectly, they tried to get him, to persuade him somehow, to accept the post of secretary of the Secretariat, and allegedly, he decidedly refused this, giving certain reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you what the reasons were?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time the assistant minister spoke, he told us that Martic had fallen under the influence of Serbia and Serbian official policy, that allegedly he wanted to form a special, separate - I remember his words very well - autonomous unit for the Serb people living in Croatia, an autonomous unit within Croatia, as he said, which would probably later become a province or a republic, and he said very decidedly that Croatia would by no means accept this, that it would not allow the parceling up of Croatia and the establishment of regional republican structures on the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the chart that the witness has drawn be given an exhibit number? And I think out of prudence it should be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The chart that the witness drew is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 283, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see there is about two minutes left in the session. I'm about to start an entirely new topic so I wonder if it would be a convenient time to break, just a couple of minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, then. Witness, we are going to break for the day today. You must come back on Monday at --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's 9 a.m., Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 9 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In Courtroom III, a different courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In Courtroom III. I guess somebody will take you there. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
